subtype: Grieving in a family with different styles [Actor]
passage: “Sit, child, sit. When my father died I was twenty-six, and the three of us grieved so differently that we nearly broke as a family. My brother Parveen took charge of every form, every phone call and every chair for the guests. My sister Tashi talked about our father all night, telling the same stories again and again. I said almost nothing and sat by the window. Tashi said, ‘Dolma doesn't even miss him.’ Parveen said, ‘Tashi is only making noise.’ Each thought the others were doing it wrong. On the eleventh night Parveen stopped in the doorway with a file in his hand and said, ‘I don't know how to sit.’ We all laughed and cried at once. That night we finally sat together.”

qa.q: How old was Dolma when the father died?
qa.a: Dolma was twenty-six when the father died.

qa.q: What might Parveen have meant when Parveen said, “I don't know how to sit”?
qa.a: Parveen probably felt that tasks were the only way to cope with the loss, and being still was frightening, so he admitted it finally.

qa.q: What could the three have done sooner to lessen the hurt?
qa.a: They could have asked each other how each was coping, and understood that quiet, talking and busy work were all ways of grieving.

qa.q: How might Tashi have felt when Tashi said, “Dolma doesn't even miss him”?
qa.a: Tashi may have felt lonely in the storytelling and frustrated that others were not joining in, and so read Dolma's silence as not caring.

grounding: An elder recalls a family whose members grieved quietly, by talking and by staying busy, each thinking the others were doing it wrong, until they understood.

subtype: Grieving in a family with different styles [Actor]
passage: The storm cut the power the night after their mother's funeral, and the three grown-up children were stuck in the old house with no phone signal. Aparna sat by the window with a candle, silent. Chinmay hunted through drawers for the property papers and bank documents. “We have to do this while everyone's here,” he said. Their younger sister Riya talked and talked, going through old photographs. “You're not even sad, Aparna,” Riya said. “And you're not doing anything useful,” said Chinmay. Aparna looked at them both. “I am sad. I don't know how to say it in your way.” Chinmay put down the files. Riya went quiet. Chinmay held the candle while Aparna lifted the photo album.

qa.q: What did Chinmay search for in the drawers?
qa.a: Chinmay hunted through drawers for the property papers and bank documents.

qa.q: Why did Aparna say, “I am sad. I don't know how to say it in your way”?
qa.a: Aparna felt misjudged, since silence looked like not grieving to the other two, and wanted them to understand that the sadness was real.

qa.q: What might the three do next to grieve better together?
qa.a: They could take turns, with a little time for papers and a little for the photographs and silence, so each style of grieving has room.

qa.q: How might Chinmay have felt when Chinmay put down the files?
qa.a: Chinmay may have felt a mixture of shame and relief at seeing Aparna's grief, and realised the papers could wait a little.

grounding: A family member grieves quietly while another talks and another keeps busy with tasks, each thinking the others are not grieving properly.

subtype: Grieving in a family with different styles [Actor]
passage: In the house near the bus stand in Sirsi, three days after Ajji died, everyone was grieving differently. Harish's sister Meenu talked about Ajji all day, to anyone who would listen. Their uncle fixed the leaking tap, swept the yard twice and argued with the milkman. Harish sat on Ajji's old cot on the verandah and barely spoke. 'He doesn't even care,' Meenu told Nazia in the kitchen. Out in the yard, the uncle muttered that Meenu was making a drama. Nazia, Harish's wife, put down the tea tray. 'Meenu, he hasn't left that cot since Tuesday. That's how he's missing her.' That evening Meenu sat beside her brother on the cot without speaking. After a long while, Harish said, 'She used to shell peas here,' and Meenu held his hand.

qa.q: What did the uncle fix?
qa.a: The leaking tap.

qa.q: What does Harish sitting on Ajji's cot for days show about how he grieves?
qa.a: He is deeply sad and missing Ajji, grieving quietly rather than by talking or keeping busy.

qa.q: How did Nazia reduce the hurt between Meenu and Harish?
qa.a: She explained that Harish's silence on the cot was his way of missing Ajji, so Meenu could understand and sit with him.

qa.q: Why did Meenu think Harish didn't care?
qa.a: Meenu grieves by talking, so his silence looked like not caring to her until Nazia explained.

grounding: A family grieves a grandmother in different ways, talking, keeping busy or staying silent, and understanding eases the hurt.

subtype: Grieving in a family with different styles [Actor]
passage: In the weeks after their mother's funeral in Malmö, Emil handled everything: the bank letters, the flowers, cancelling her phone contract, sorting her books into boxes. His sister Layla wanted to talk about Mamma every evening, watching old videos, laughing and crying. Their father went for long walks alone and came back silent. One night Layla snapped, 'You're acting like she was a to-do list!' Emil threw a pen across the table. 'Someone has to do it!' Then their father said quietly from the doorway, 'I walk. You work. Layla talks. We're all missing the same person.' The kitchen went still. Emil sat down, and for the first time he let Layla play one of the videos. He watched it to the end.

qa.q: What did the father do after the funeral?
qa.a: He went for long walks alone and came back silent.

qa.q: Why did Emil throw the pen when Layla snapped?
qa.a: Emil felt hurt and misunderstood, grieving through tasks, and angry at being told it looked like not caring.

qa.q: How did the father's words help the family?
qa.a: By naming each style, walking, working and talking, as grief for the same person, so they stopped judging each other.

qa.q: How might Layla feel when Emil finally watches the video?
qa.a: She likely feels relieved and closer to him, seeing that he is grieving too.

grounding: A family grieving a mother clashes over different styles until the father names them as the same loss.

subtype: Grieving in a family with different styles [Actor]
passage: In the hospital family room, the morning after Sachin's father died, three people grieved in three directions. Sachin's younger brother, Nikhil, was on the phone nonstop: the crematorium, the priest, the relatives in Indore, a list growing on his palm in blue ink. Nazia, Sachin's wife, kept trying to talk. "Remember how he sang in the car?" she said, twice. Sachin sat by the window and said nothing. Inside, he was furious with both of them. How could Nikhil think about timings? Why did Nazia need words? Around noon Nikhil snapped, "Could you at least help, bhaiya?" Sachin nearly shouted back. Then he saw his brother's hands shaking over the list. He took the phone. "You call the family. I'll call the priest." Later, in the corridor, he told Nazia, "I can't talk yet. Stay close anyway?" She nodded and held his arm.

qa.q: What was Nikhil writing on his palm?
qa.a: A list of calls, the crematorium, the priest and the relatives in Indore, growing on his palm in blue ink.

qa.q: What was Sachin feeling as he sat by the window?
qa.a: He was grieving silently and also angry, judging Nikhil for thinking about timings and Nazia for needing words.

qa.q: What helped the three of them grieve side by side?
qa.a: Sachin noticed Nikhil's shaking hands and shared the calls, and told Nazia plainly that he couldn't talk yet but wanted her close.

qa.q: How might Nazia have seen Sachin's silence?
qa.a: She may have felt shut out and worried that he was not grieving at all, until he explained and asked her to stay close.

grounding: Shows one family grieving in different styles, quiet, talking and keeping busy, where understanding each style reduces hurt.
